issues.issue: The Effective Date is left blank ("as of the _ day of [ ]"), so the date from which the Agreement and its representations run cannot be fixed from the text. That blank is a mechanical defect a court would have to fill by construction.
The undefined Effective Date matters because Section 3's chapeau makes the Company's representations effective "as of the Effective Date"; but this is a gap rather than a contradiction.

Undefined terms are given the Operating Agreement's meanings, while paragraph 5.1 supplies its own definitions of "Affiliate" and related terms "for purposes of this Article 5 and elsewhere as specified", leaving which definition governs elsewhere unresolved. A court could be asked to reconcile the preamble with 5.1.

"Notes shall be purchased in units of $1.00" and a minimum of "20,000 Units or U.S. $20,000" use "Units", a term not defined in this Agreement. The reference is thin but the arithmetic makes its meaning plain.

"Loan Amount" is defined as the amount required to be loaned, yet the same paragraph makes it adjustable for "the accrual and payment of interest and principal", so it is unclear whether Loan Amount tracks principal or a running balance. Because payments under 1.4(c) turn on "relative principal amounts", the distinction has consequences.

The roll-over right is conditioned on the Noteholder being a "qualified investor at the time of the request", a term used but never defined in the Agreement (Section 4.1 uses "accredited investor" instead). A court would have to decide which standard governs.

The "Floating Rate" is set unilaterally "in the sole discretion of the Company" subject to quarterly adjustment, but the floor is stated as "not less than eight percent (8.00%) on an annualized basis for such calendar year", mixing a quarterly reset with an annual measuring period. Whether the 8% floor is tested quarterly or over the calendar year is genuinely uncertain.

Prepayment on request is available "on the last day of any quarter during or after which all of the following conditions have been satisfied", which is awkward as to whether conditions must be met before or within the quarter. The ambiguity is small but real.

The condition turns on the Company's "sole and absolute discretion" that prepayment "will not adversely affect the Company's obligations or liquidity", a standard with no benchmark and no good-faith qualifier. A court could be asked whether any implied limit constrains that discretion.

The paragraph refers to "the Holding Period", whereas 1.4(a)(ii)(A) defines only a "Minimum Holding Period"; the mismatched term is a mechanical slip. Its meaning is nonetheless recoverable from context.

Selective prepayment of certain Noteholders' Notes sits against the ratable-payment covenant in 6.1(b) and the pro rata rule in 1.4(c), though both are expressed as subject to 1.4. The carve-out largely resolves the tension.

The pro rata payment rule is made "subject to" 1.4(a)-(b), which permit wholly discretionary and selective prepayments, so the rule can be displaced at will. A court could be asked how far 1.4(b) may swallow 1.4(c) and 6.1(b).

The proviso protects a Noteholder against an amendment with "discriminatory application" to his Note, a phrase that is nowhere defined and could cover any non-uniform effect. The scope of that protection is genuinely contestable.

This 50%-of-principal amendment mechanic for the Notes sits alongside paragraph 10.5, which requires Company approval and a "Majority in Interest" for modifications of the Agreement, and the two consent regimes could overlap. The subject matters differ, which mostly reconciles them.

The clause says the Company may re-issue Notes "and then only upon the condition that the original Note is returned", which sits oddly with the following sentence requiring issuance of a replacement for a lost or destroyed Note. The reader must decide whether the return condition applies to replacements too.

The Closing Account must be "segregated from the Company's general bank accounts" and held "exclusively" for investor funds, yet the same paragraph contemplates funds "held ... by the Company" during the Pre-Qualification Period. Whether segregation is absolute is arguable.

This paragraph speaks of amending the "proposed Note Subscription Amount" and returning funds exceeding the "Note Subscription Amount approved by the Company", while 2.2(a) frames subscription and acceptance in terms of the "Loan Amount". The two labels are used interchangeably without a stated equivalence.

The Schedule is called "SCHEDULE A" here but the preamble and paragraph 1.1 call it the "Schedule of Purchasers attached hereto", and the exhibit list names only a "Schedule of Purchasers". The inconsistent label is minor and readily harmonised.

The promise of a security interest in the Company's assets is qualified out of existence by 5.3(a), which lets the Manager grant liens senior to the Lien and subordinate Noteholder remedies. A court could be asked whether 2.3(a) leaves the Noteholders any secured position.

The clause subordinates "the lien on the Fund's assets", but "Fund" is not a defined term anywhere in the Agreement, which uses "Company" throughout. The slip is small but goes to the description of the collateral.

Blanket subordination to "any Company Borrowings" is hard to square with 6.2(b), which forbids the Company to permit any Lien on the Collateral without a Majority in Interest except as permitted with respect to a Company Borrowing. Which provision controls the extent of permitted senior liens is arguable.

This funding mechanic covers only commitments under 1.2(c) and 1.2(d), but 1.2(b) directs that Noteholder-requested increases be "funded as provided in paragraph 2.4 below". The cross-references do not match up.
The Company is a Delaware LLC yet the representation is of "requisite corporate power", a mismatch of legal vocabulary. It is a drafting slip unlikely to change meaning.

The representation covers "the Series of Notes to be issued in such closing", but "Series" is not a defined concept and the Agreement elsewhere treats the Notes as a single undifferentiated class. Whether Notes are issued in distinct series matters to ratable payment and voting.
The carve-out for violations "that would not have a material adverse effect on the Company" supplies no measure of materiality. Such qualifiers are standard but their boundary is contestable.

The purpose clause reaches "such other related activities" as the Manager "deems reasonably necessary or appropriate", a catch-all sitting against an enumerated list of lending and foreclosure activities. Its outer limit is uncertain.

The representation that Portfolio Loans are secured by property located "primarily in the United States" sits against 6.1(g), which contemplates loans where foreign-secured Portfolio Loans exceed twenty percent. The two provisions pull in different directions on geography.

The covenant to use proceeds "solely for the operations of its business" is far narrower than 5.2, by which the Purchasers consent to use of proceeds "for any purpose not prohibited by the Operating Agreement". The two use-of-proceeds provisions are hard to reconcile.

The disclaimer that the Company and Manager "owe no fiduciary or similar duties" leaves the reach of "similar duties" undefined, and does not say whether it displaces implied covenants or duties arising under the Operating Agreement. That scope is exactly the sort of term litigants fight over.

A blanket no-duty statement is in tension with the express arm's-length and fairness obligations imposed on the Manager in 5.7(e), 5.8 and the covenants in 6.1. A court could be asked whether 4.3 nullifies those protections.

"Affiliate" turns on undefined "control", and the definition is expressly limited to "this Article 5 and elsewhere as specified in this Agreement" while "Affiliate" is used in 9(c) and 10.8 without any such specification. Both the control test and the definition's reach are open.

Excluding "any Noteholder or a limited partner or non-voting member of a Sponsored Investment Fund" from "Affiliate" cuts against 5.8's final sentence, which contemplates Noteholders who "are also Affiliates of the Manager or Servicer". The carve-out and that sentence do not sit easily together.

"Private Client" reaches "any investor or client or their Affiliates for whom the Manager or its Affiliates provides loan or real estate brokerage, investment or lending services", a boundary the Manager can enlarge simply by providing services. Because Private Client status switches off the restrictions in 5.7(b)(i)-(iii), the definition's reach matters.

"Sponsored Investment Fund" sweeps in any fund "sponsored, promoted, owned or managed now or in the future by the Manager or its Affiliates" and names R.E. Loans, LLC expressly, so the label attaches to the Manager's own affiliated vehicles. Whether that status was meant to strip such entities of affiliate treatment is genuinely contestable.

Because 5.7(e) excludes loans to a Sponsored Investment Fund from "Related Party Loan", this definition lets loans to the Manager's own affiliated funds escape the 20% cap in 5.7(e)(ii) and the arm's-length conditions in 5.7(e)(i). That is difficult to reconcile with the Agreement's evident scheme of restricting affiliate lending.

Consent is given to use of proceeds "for any purpose not prohibited by the Operating Agreement", an open-ended standard defined by reference to a separate document the Company may amend. The limit on the Company's use of investor money is therefore hard to locate.
This open consent is inconsistent with 3.8, under which the Company "shall use the proceeds of the Loan solely for the operations of its business". A court would have to decide which governs.

The clause says the Purchasers agree to "the provisions of paragraphs 5.2(a)-(f)", but paragraph 5.2 has no subparagraphs; the lettered provisions are in 5.3. That mis-citation leaves the object of the agreement to be supplied by construction.

The reference to authority "pursuant to the terms of the Operating Agreement and the Act" conflicts with paragraph 3.6, which defines "the Act" as the Securities Act of 1933, whereas here it must mean the Delaware LLC Act. The defined term and its use point in different directions.

The Manager may agree to whatever subordination and standstill terms it "may deem commercially reasonable", a self-judged standard with no external benchmark. Its content would be the battleground in any dispute about a subordination.

Authorising liens senior to the Lien and terms that "subordinate or otherwise restrict the rights of the Noteholders" is hard to reconcile with 2.3(a)'s grant of a security interest to the Noteholders and 6.2(b)'s prohibition on permitting Liens on the Collateral. Read at full width this paragraph can hollow out the security bargained for.

Transactions are permitted if "within the general scope and purpose of the Company", a boundary that is nowhere fixed and that the Manager judges in its sole discretion. The catch-all "or other persons" at the end of an enumerated list adds to the uncertainty.

The broad sole-discretion permission is qualified only by "except to the extent prohibited by this Agreement", leaving its relation to the specific affiliate conditions in 5.7 to be worked out. The specific conditions would normally prevail, which reduces the tension.

The unrestricted Co-Lending permission must be read with 6.1(f), which requires commercially reasonable efforts to prevent a Co-Lending Activity from constituting a security, and with 5.8's arm's-length proviso. The qualifier "except to the extent prohibited by this Agreement" mostly reconciles them.

This paragraph lets the Company sell foreclosed property to the Manager and Affiliates "on such terms and conditions as the Manager, in its sole discretion, determines", while 5.7(b) imposes marketing, pricing and commission conditions on precisely those sales. The general permission and the specific conditions must be reconciled.

Sole-discretion purchases and sales of Portfolio Loans with Affiliates sit against the specific pricing and underwriting conditions in 5.7(c) and 5.7(d) for the same transactions. The saving words "except to the extent prohibited by this Agreement" leave the relationship to be construed.

The cap on Loan Services compensation is measured by fees "payable pursuant to paragraphs 5.4(b)-(f)", yet 5.4 states those fees are payable to the Manager or its designee, not necessarily to the Servicer, and 5.6 lets Affiliates keep further compensation outright. Whether the cap is effective is arguable.

The chapeau says the Company "shall be entitled to pay" fees, which reads as a permission rather than an obligation, while the listed items are stated as fixed entitlements. Whether the fees are mandatory or discretionary is left open.

The fee list defines a "Management Fee" in 5.4(a), but 6.2(c) forbids paying salaries in any month in which a "Portfolio Management Fee" is payable, a term defined nowhere. The mismatch of labels affects when 6.2(c) bites.

"Company Expenses" is defined by a broad list closing with "any extraordinary expenses of the Company", an open-ended catch-all against enumerated specifics. Its outer reach against the carve-out for Loan Services expenses is contestable.

The exclusion of Loan Services expenses, which "shall be borne by the Manager or the Servicer", must be squared with 5.3(f), which caps Servicer compensation and refers reimbursable expenses back to this paragraph. The circular cross-reference invites argument.

The paragraph defines "Permitted Expenses" to include "the foregoing expenses and indemnifications", although no indemnification is mentioned in this paragraph and the defined term is never used again in the Agreement. The definition is left without work to do.

Indemnification is extended to "the members, officers, employees, and consultants of the Company", but the proviso excluding willful misconduct or gross negligence is framed by reference to "the Manager's duties under the operating agreement". The conduct standard does not match the class of indemnitees.

The catch-all "or similar compensation for services" following an enumerated list of construction, brokerage, property management and development fees leaves the sweep of the Manager's retained compensation uncertain. The list-plus-catch-all structure is exactly the ejusdem generis problem.

Letting the Manager keep fees "received ... with respect to an entity in which the Company has a debt or equity interest" is difficult to square with 5.4, which purports to state the amounts and times at which the Company pays the Manager. Whether 5.4 is an exhaustive compensation scheme is arguable.

The Loan Origination Fee is "in an amount determined on a case-by-case basis", which fixes no limit at all on affiliate compensation. Read with 5.6, which makes such fees the Manager's property, the absence of any cap is a live construction point.

The condition requires "commercially reasonable efforts to sell any property ... at a fair price on the open market for at least ninety (90) days", with neither "commercially reasonable efforts" nor "fair price" defined. Both are standards a buyer and a lender would apply differently.

The price constraints can be mutually unsatisfiable: the price must be "no higher than the independently appraised value" yet "no lower than the total amount of the Company's 'investment'", which may exceed appraised value in a foreclosure. The provision gives no rule for that case.

Permitted commissions are those "customarily provided for such services to third parties in connection with like kind transactions in the geographic area", a standard with no fixed content. Its application would turn on evidence rather than text.

By disapplying clauses (i)-(iii) to sales to Sponsored Investment Funds and Private Clients, this sub-clause removes the marketing, best-price and no-commission protections from the very affiliated buyers 5.7(b) was drafted to police. The exception is hard to reconcile with the restriction it qualifies.

The condition reads "the borrower shall not be default under the loan", omitting "in"; the sense is recoverable but the sentence is ungrammatical. It also leaves unstated whether non-monetary defaults count.
The test is whether the loan satisfies underwriting criteria "customarily applied by the Company", criteria the Company itself sets and can change. The benchmark is self-referential and unfixed.

The disclaimer that no affiliate is "obligated to purchase any loans from the Company" is expressly excepted by 5.7(e)(iii), which requires the Manager to buy defaulted Related Party Loans; the two must be read together. The express carve-out largely resolves it.

"Related Party Loan" is triggered only where "the borrower is an Affiliate", and "Affiliate" in 5.1(a) expressly excludes Noteholders and non-voting members of Sponsored Investment Funds. The gateway definition therefore controls the whole of 5.7(e) and its boundary is arguable.

The cap is set at twenty percent "of the Loan Portfolio", a term defined in 5.4(a) as the aggregate principal of outstanding Portfolio Loans measured monthly, so the denominator and the moment of measurement are not obviously the same as "immediately after making or purchasing". How the cap is computed is genuinely open.

The cap is largely defeated by the unnumbered exclusion at the end of 5.7(e), which provides that a Related Party Loan does not include any loan to a Sponsored Investment Fund or Private Client as defined in 5.1(c) and 5.1(b). Whether the cap constrains lending to the Manager's own affiliated funds cannot be answered from this sub-clause alone.

The repurchase obligation is triggered by "any material event of default ... continuing for ninety (90) consecutive days", with materiality undefined and no mechanism for determining it. Whether the obligation has been triggered would be litigable on the facts.

The exclusion removes from "Related Party Loan" any loan whose borrower is a Sponsored Investment Fund or Private Client, categories defined in 5.1(b)-(c) to include entities owned or managed by the Manager. Whether such a loan is nonetheless a loan to an "Affiliate" under 5.7(e) is precisely the kind of question a court is asked to resolve.

Read literally the exclusion cancels the arm's-length standard in 5.7(e)(i), the twenty percent cap in 5.7(e)(ii) and the repurchase duty in 5.7(e)(iii) for the Manager's own sponsored vehicles, leaving 5.7(e) with little operation. That is a whole-instrument incoherence with the affiliate-lending scheme of Article 5.

Making Advance liens subordinate to "the Lien securing the Notes" assumes the Lien has priority, while 2.3(b) and 5.3(a) subordinate that Lien to any Company Borrowings. The ranking of the three tiers is workable but not spelled out.

The proviso requires terms "no less advantageous to the Company than if such loan ... were made pursuant to an arm's length transaction" with a comparable non-affiliate, a comparison that depends entirely on extrinsic evidence. The standard is real but its application is contestable.

The last sentence subjects Noteholders who are "also Affiliates of the Manager or Servicer" to 5.7, yet 5.1(a) expressly excludes any Noteholder from the definition of "Affiliate". The two provisions cannot both be given full effect.

The statement that "no provision of this Agreement shall be deemed to prohibit" outside businesses is in tension with the express restrictions on affiliate dealings in 5.7 and the covenants in 6.1 and 6.2. Read broadly it would override provisions elsewhere in the instrument.

Sub-paragraph (g) is an affirmative covenant "[t]o make any mortgage loan, if ... aggregate principal of Portfolio Loans secured by real property located outside the United States ... exceeds twenty percent", which is nonsense unless a negative such as "not" was omitted. The mechanical error inverts the covenant's meaning.

The chapeau to Article 6 conditions all these covenants on the absence of contrary written consent from a majority of Noteholders, while 6.1's own opening sentence states the covenants apply "[u]ntil the satisfaction of its obligation to pay principal and interest" without that qualification. The two openings state different conditions for the same covenants.

Sub-paragraph (c) forbids paying salaries in any month in which a "Portfolio Management Fee" is payable, but 5.4(a) defines the monthly fee as the "Management Fee" and no "Portfolio Management Fee" is defined anywhere. Whether the prohibition ever operates depends on equating the two labels.

The covenant bars amendments that "materially and adversely effect[] the economic interests of the Noteholders", using "effects" for "affects" and leaving "economic interests" undefined. Both the verb and the standard would need construing.

This restriction sits against the preamble, which incorporates the Operating Agreement "as it may be amended from time to time" without qualification, so amendments could alter defined terms used throughout this Agreement. The two provisions address amendment power differently.

Transfers are permitted only "to qualified investors", a term used here and in 1.2(d) but never defined, while Section 4.1 speaks instead of "accredited investor". The transfer condition therefore has no fixed content.

Clause (iii) authorises filings needed "to comply with state or federal securities with respect to the issuance of the Notes", omitting the word "laws". The omission is obvious but leaves the grant's scope to be supplied.

The power is declared "irrevocable" and to survive death or assignment "for the sole purpose of enabling the Manager to execute ... any instrument necessary to effect such transfer", so it is unclear whether the limiting purpose qualifies survival generally or only after assignment. The sentence can be parsed two ways.

The covenant extends to documents "necessary or expedient" and to whatever is "necessary or appropriate in the judgment of the Manager", a standard set by the Manager alone. The obligation's outer limit is undefined.

The Collateral Agent's powers are "such powers and authority as may be granted in the Security Agreement", so this paragraph's content depends on a document whose terms are not set out here. Its priority-of-payment rule is also stated in general terms only.

Making the Collateral Agent's actions "binding on the Noteholders" while the Manager appoints and instructs it is in tension with 4.3's statement that the Company and Manager owe no duties to Noteholders and with 10.6's preservation of each Noteholder's remedies. Whether Noteholders retain individual enforcement rights is arguable.

The Collateral Agent is to act "on terms required by Manager", including consenting to subordination, although 9(a) appoints it to "represent the Noteholders" and 9(c) makes it non-affiliated. The representative role and the Manager's control cannot both be given full effect.
The clause binds "successors and assigns" although Section 7 makes the Notes non-negotiable and non-assignable without Company consent. The provisions are conventional and readily harmonised.

Delaware law is chosen here, while 10.8(d) measures counsel's conduct by "the California Rules of Professional Conduct or similar and applicable rules in any other jurisdiction". The choice-of-law clause and the conflicts waiver point to different bodies of rules.

The clause bars modifications "effective with respect to all Purchasers" without a Majority in Interest, yet allows any single Noteholder to modify "any provision of this Agreement with respect to his own Note" with the Manager's consent alone. How far individual side-modifications can go is left open.

Paragraph 1.5 lets holders of more than fifty percent of unpaid principal amend the Notes with the Company's consent, while this paragraph requires the Company plus a "Majority in Interest" for the Agreement. The overlapping consent thresholds would have to be reconciled.

Preserving each Noteholder's cumulative remedies is in tension with Section 9, which makes the Collateral Agent's actions binding on the Noteholders and channels enforcement of the Collateral through it. The provisions address different remedies, which mostly reconciles them.

The integration clause lists the Agreement, Exhibits, Subscription Agreement, Security Agreement and Notes, but omits the private placement memorandum on which 4.1(b) requires each Purchaser to represent it relied. Whether the memorandum is outside the bargain is a real question.

The paragraph redefines "Noteholder" for 10.8 and 10.9 to "also include its principals, employees, agents or Affiliates", expanding who is bound by the conflict waivers beyond the actual signatory. That extension is contestable.

The disclaimer that Company Counsel does not represent the Noteholders is difficult to square with 10.9(a) and 10.9(b), which contemplate Greenberg Traurig representing Noteholders and even simultaneously representing a Noteholder and the Company. Whether counsel ever acted for a Noteholder is left uncertain by the instrument read as a whole.

The Noteholder waives "any present conflict of interest", which on its face does not reach conflicts arising later, yet the paragraph consents to representation in "any and all Company Legal Matters (including any dispute ... with ... one or more Noteholders)" that could only arise in the future. The temporal scope of the waiver is genuinely ambiguous.

The consent to Company Counsel representing Noteholders "in matters unrelated to the Transactions" sits against 10.8(b)'s flat statement that Company Counsel "is not representing, and will not represent, the Noteholders". The line between related and unrelated matters is left for construction.

The consent is given "subject to the specific consent of the Noteholder holding the Other Noteholder Portfolio Interest", so a general advance consent is made conditional on a later particular one without saying what happens if it is withheld. The waiver's operative effect is uncertain.

The party acknowledges it "has been informed of and has had an opportunity to ask for and have obtained information relevant to such representation, including disclosure of the reasonably foreseeable adverse consequences", without identifying what was disclosed. Whether that amounts to informed consent is contestable on the words used.

The legend permits transfer on an effective registration statement or an opinion of counsel, whereas Section 7 makes the Notes non-negotiable and bars any transfer without the Company's consent "withheld in its sole and absolute discretion". The two transfer regimes state different conditions.
